paras: The threat against Galveston barber T. H. Thomas was a death threat that, by his own account, white residents of Galveston, Texas, made to Thomas, a Black barber, in August 1900 before he left for the National Negro Business Men's League convention in Boston. Thomas told the convention that the callers had promised to kill him on his return if he went in the interest of Lillian Clayton Jewett's anti-lynching league. No violence against him was reported, but the published account caused severe criticism of him at home, and a later dispatch said he hesitated to return for fear of a noose.

Thomas was a delegate to the first convention of the National Negro Business Men's League, held in Boston in late August 1900. He spoke on barbering, describing his rise from a poor bootblack to proprietor of shops employing 12 or 14 men. At the time, Jewett, the head of an anti-lynching league in Boston, was receiving a heavy mail, much of it blaming her for riots in New York and Ohio and some of it threatening.

According to a Boston dispatch of August 24, Thomas said he had earned the respect of white Galveston residents, and that when his trip became known "a number of white citizens called on him." They told him they wished him "God speed" if he went to better the industrial condition of Black people, but would kill him "as soon as you set foot in Galveston" if he went in the interest of Jewett and her league. The Fredericksburg Free Lance attributed the same words to a single "Galveston, Tex, white man."

The New York Sun wrote that the delegates applauded the remark, and that it was unclear whether the applause was an intentional rebuke of Jewett. The Free Lance said the story "created a sensation" and was the first reference at the convention to Jewett's crusade.

A Boston dispatch of September 1 reported that Thomas had received word that the published quotations had caused "very severe criticism" in Galveston, where they were read as showing he favored the Jewett movement. The same dispatch said Thomas had in fact spoken strongly against the Jewett league and called it unwise for Black business men to be identified with it. The Sun's version added that he hesitated to return "for fear that a noose will be awaiting his arrival" and was anxious to go home "in a peaceful frame of mind." No report of violence against Thomas after his return appears in the coverage.

The first report ran in the New York Sun on August 25 under the headline "NEGRO OBJECTS TO MISS JEWETT," which presented the threat as a mark against Jewett rather than as an attack on Thomas. The Free Lance used the story to open an item titled "Miss Jewett Becomes Nervous." The September 1 follow-up wire spread more widely, appearing in Washington, Waterbury, Houston, Wichita, Americus, Marion and De Queen under headlines such as "MR. THOMAS WAS MISQUOTED" and "IS NOT A JEWETT ADHERENT."

The Houston Daily Post, the only Texas paper found carrying the story, printed only the disavowal under "THOMAS ENTERS A DENIAL" and referred to "the Jewett woman." The Sun's "NEGRO THOMAS AFRAID TO GO HOME" was reprinted in Honolulu's Pacific Commercial Advertiser on September 19. In the Black press, the Colored American's convention report listed Thomas's paper on barbering but did not mention the threat, and no Black-press account of the threat or the disavowal was found.

Accounts differ on who made the threat: the Sun's first dispatch described "a number of white citizens," while the Free Lance named one white man. The papers also differ on Thomas's initials, giving J. A. (the Sun's lead and the Free Lance), T. T. (the Springfield Republican) and T. H. (the Sun's program, the Colored American and the follow-up wire). The "misquoted" dispatches disputed the impression that Thomas supported Jewett, not his report of the threat, which they restated.

reader.title: Threat against Galveston barber T. H. Thomas
bases: The papers report a death threat delivered to a Black barber by white Galveston residents before he left for a Boston convention, with no violence reported (A1, A5, A7).
No one was killed; the episode is a reported threat to kill Thomas, made by 'a number of white citizens' (A1) or by one 'white man' (A5), if he worked for Jewett's anti-lynching league.
Every report of the threat traces to Thomas's own speech in Boston (A1, A5), and the later dispatches describe how he was quoted rather than confirming the threat independently (A6, A7).

accounts.label: Thomas's speech as first reported
accounts.gist: White Galveston residents told Thomas they wished him well if he went to Boston to better Black business conditions, but would kill him on his return if he went in the interest of Jewett's league.

accounts.label: Boston follow-up wire
accounts.gist: The published quotations caused severe criticism of Thomas in Galveston, where they were read as pro-Jewett; Thomas said he had spoken strongly against the Jewett league, and the Sun added that he feared a noose awaited him.

accounts.label: Convention reports
accounts.gist: Two reports of the convention name Thomas as speaking on barbering and on his own rise in business, without mentioning a threat.

framing.detail: The Sun headed the first dispatch 'NEGRO OBJECTS TO MISS JEWETT' and presented the applause as a possible rebuke of Jewett.
The Free Lance headed its item 'Miss Jewett Becomes Nervous' and tied the threat to the threatening letters she was receiving.
The Sept. 1 wire ran under headlines stressing Thomas's disavowal, such as 'MR. THOMAS WAS MISQUOTED' and the Houston Post's 'THOMAS ENTERS A DENIAL'.
The Sun's follow-up, 'NEGRO THOMAS AFRAID TO GO HOME', described him as 'in a dilemma' and fearing a noose, and was reprinted in Honolulu.
The Colored American listed Thomas's paper on barbering in its convention report without mentioning the threat.

conflicts.note: The Sun's own Aug. 25 program list gives 'T. H. Thomas, Galveston, Tex.' for barbering, as do the Black-press report and the Sept. 1 wire; T. H. is the better-supported form.
Both versions derive from Thomas's speech.
